newsitem.title: UK: Gold aims higher, picking up momentum above $345.
newsitem.headline: Gold aims higher, picking up momentum above $345.

text.p: Gold cruised to its highest fix in five weeks on Friday afternoon as the dollar's weakness and physical offtake prompted fund buying, dealers said.
Having overcome the $345.00 barrier, spot bullion secured an afternoon fix of $345.85 an ounce, the highest since April 14 and after $344.80 in the morning. It was up $2.20 from Thursday.
"I think it's just a reflection of physical demand that is clearly going on, and it caught the market a little bit short," said a dealer. "And maybe a few people are trying to get long."
This week's slide in the dollar against the yen lifted gold to a new platform from its $340-$344 range.
The dollar took a fresh lurch lower on Friday, near one-month lows at 1.6917 against the mark and dipping below 121.50 yen amid scaled-back interest rate expectations.
This, as well as illiquidity in platinum and palladium markets as a result of delays in Russian shipments, suddenly boosted prospects across the precious metals sector.
Gold had been stuck between $339-$343 since mid-April in a market cowed by the threat of selling by central banks and other institutions from reserves of over 36,000 tonnes.

But though further gains appeared to be on the cards, gold was likely to hit somewhat sterile ground above $350. Analysts said this level would attract a plethora of selling that had been waiting for higher prices.
"Above $350 there is going to be good selling," said one.
Silver also picked up on the weaker dollar, rallying around 10 cents on Thursday and adding three more on Friday to $4.84/$4.86.
The session saw some borrowing activity that firmed lease rates slightly, but for a good upside run silver needed to finish above $4.85 resistance, analysts said.
Palladium caught the spotlight again as it fixed at a two-year high of $164.50 an ounce, up from $162.50 in the morning and compared to Thursday's finish of $158.40/$159.40.
Its sister metal platinum was fixed at $383.50, its highest setting since March 5 this year.
"Supplies are so tight that it is cheaper to buy spot metal than borrow it," one dealer said.

Prices of both metals have risen rapidly this year since Russia, the world's biggest exporter of palladium and second biggest exporter of platinum, had been unable to resume talks with Japan, the biggest importer of both, on a 1997 supply contract. Shipments have been stalled since December.
But the white metals were also buoyed by heavy speculative involvement based on a bullish hunch.
